meta.reportLabel: PAYROLLS BLEW UP THE DOVISH CASE - AND CANADA BLEW UP A LEG OF THIS BOARD. US August non-farm payrolls printed +162,000 against a +53,000 consensus, roughly triple expectations, WITH the prior two months revised up by a combined 55,000 - July went from MINUS 23,000 to PLUS 21,000. Unemployment held 4.1%, average hourly earnings +0.3% m/m and 3.1% y/y, participation rose to 61.6%. The labour-market-collapse story that was the entire dovish case has been revised away. September pricing swung back from roughly 50-55% to 55-62% depending on venue, the 2-year yield hit its highest since January 2025, gold fell 2% intraday to 4,432.56 and silver to 65.990. USD moves 0 to PLUS 1 - but only plus 1, because Waller said explicitly his hold case keys off INFLATION not payrolls, so CPI on September 11 still decides the meeting. Canada went the other way in the same minute: employment MINUS 41,700 against a +15,000 consensus after +75,100, full-time MINUS 35,900, wage growth decelerating. The BoC leg of the CAD trade broke; the oil leg did not - WTI 91.48, +9.7% on the week, its best week since mid-July. CAD comes DOWN from +2 to +1 and USD/CAD goes from HIGH SHORT to RANGE. Sterling lost its own trigger the dovish way: the DMP survey printed one-year CPI expectations at 3.1%, DOWN from 3.4%, and BoE September 17 is now 90% priced for a hold. Over the weekend the war escalated materially: the IRGC fired ballistic missiles at a US carrier and destroyer on September 5 and CENTCOM destroyed or disabled three Iranian tankers in response. Board: JPY, AUD, EUR +2; USD, CAD, CHF +1; GBP, NZD 0. Cleanest: GBP/JPY SHORT, GBP/AUD SHORT, AUD/NZD LONG, NZD/JPY SHORT, EUR/GBP LONG. US CPI Friday and the ECB Thursday are the week.

meta.regime: The regime is still seven-of-eight central banks responding to an energy-led inflation impulse, but two of the legs this file has been leaning on were tested on Friday and one of them failed. The dollar is no longer the automatic funding currency: a +162,000 payroll with 55,000 of upward revisions removed the labour-market-collapse premise that Waller built his hold case on, and the dollar earns a genuine upgrade to +1. Canada is the mirror image - the oil leg is stronger than ever after crude put in its best week since mid-July and the war escalated again over the weekend, but the central-bank leg is damaged by a 41,700 job loss and cooling wages, so CAD comes back to +1 and the trades that leaned on it lose conviction. What survives untouched is the no-dollar core: the BoJ, RBA and ECB calls all hardened while the BoE lost its hawkish trigger, which is why the cleanest expressions on this board remain sterling shorts against yen and Aussie.
meta.nextBigEvent: US August CPI on Friday September 11 at 12:30Z, headline consensus 3.4%, with PPI the day before on September 10 at 12:30Z. This is now THE event of the cycle rather than a confirmation: Waller stated his hold case is conditioned on inflation continuing to improve and explicitly not on monthly payroll numbers, so a +162,000 jobs print does not by itself flip him - a cool CPI keeps a sitting Governor arguing for a hold five days before the FOMC and caps the dollar at +1, while a hot one hands Warsh the meeting and takes the dollar through the week's highs against everything except the yen. The ECB decision on Thursday September 10 at 12:15Z sits in between: the 25bp move to a 2.50% deposit facility is fully priced on TE's own calendar, so the euro trades the guidance and the December question, which the market currently splits about 50/50 for a further move to 2.75%. Japan average cash earnings lands first, at 23:50Z on September 7.

dailyRead: Friday resolved the two-sided dollar into something closer to one-sided, and it did it with a number big enough that it cannot be dismissed as noise. US August non-farm payrolls printed +162,000 against a +53,000 consensus - roughly triple expectations - and the revisions did more damage to the dovish case than the headline did: the prior two months were revised up by a combined 55,000, with July going from MINUS 23,000 to PLUS 21,000. Unemployment held at 4.1%, average hourly earnings rose 0.3% m/m and 3.1% y/y, private payrolls added 127,000, government 35,000, and the participation rate ROSE to 61.6% from 61.4%, which is the detail that matters most - the unemployment rate held steady while more people entered the labour force, which is what an economy absorbing supply looks like, not one shedding jobs. For a week this file has run the argument that the Fed's data was missing while its rhetoric turned hawkish; that premise is now gone. September pricing swung back from the roughly 50-55% Waller left it at to 55-62% depending on venue, the 2-year Treasury yield touched its highest level since January 2025, gold fell more than 2% intraday to settle 4,432.56 and silver 1.45% to 65.990. USD is upgraded from 0 to +1. It is upgraded by one notch and not two for a specific reason that most desks glossed over on the day: Waller's public case for a hold was explicitly conditioned on INFLATION continuing to improve, not on the monthly payroll number, and he named three-month annualised core PCE at 3.05% versus 4.76% in February as his evidence. A jobs beat does not automatically move him. So the FOMC on September 16 is still knife-edge and the resolving input is now US CPI on Friday September 11, headline consensus 3.4%, with PPI on the 10th. That is why the dollar gets a data upgrade rather than a directional promotion. Canada is where a leg of this board actually broke, and it broke in the same minute. August employment fell 41,700 against a +15,000 consensus after +75,100 in July, with full-time employment down 35,900 and part-time down 5,800; losses ran through business and building support services at -2.8%, natural resources -2.3%, utilities -3.5% and public administration -0.7%, with only manufacturing adding at +1.2%. Wage growth decelerated. The unemployment rate did hold at 6.4%, its lowest since 2024, and participation slipped to 65.0%, so this is not a collapse - but it is enough that near-term BoC hike expectations have thinned materially, and the honest thing to say is that the CENTRAL-BANK leg of the Canada trade is the one that failed while the COMMODITY leg is stronger than it has been all cycle. WTI settled 91.48 for a weekly gain of about 9.7%, its best week since mid-July, with Brent at 96.28 and +21.18% on the month. CAD therefore comes down from +2 to +1 rather than staying or collapsing, and USD/CAD - which this file carried as a HIGH-conviction SHORT and the best dollar trade on the board - is downgraded to RANGE. That call was wrong on Friday and the specific fact that broke it was the jobs print, not the oil price. Sterling lost its own catalyst, and lost it in the dovish direction. The Decision Maker Panel survey published alongside Bailey on Friday put one-year firm CPI expectations at 3.1%, DOWN from 3.4%, which is the exact print this file named as the thing that would either hand Pill, Greene and Mann a fourth vote or take the hawkish case off the table. It took it off the table. Market-implied probability of no change on September 17 is now about 90%. GBP stays at 0 and stays the cleanest funding leg on the board, which is precisely why GBP/JPY and GBP/AUD remain the two highest-conviction trades here. The yen was the week's outperformer and nothing in the last two sessions changed that. USD/JPY fell 2.38% on the week to 156.254, having touched roughly 155.28 intraday - a one-month high for the yen and, on some measures, close to seven-month lows for the pair. Ueda has hinted that a hike is likely when the board convenes on September 17-18, saying he will decide with upside price risks in mind and that he hopes to discuss whether the likelihood of the BoJ scenario materialising is heightening; TE's own forecast for the meeting is 1.25%; Bessent has publicly pressed for decisive action. JPY holds at +2. The standing caveat also holds and is unchanged: July household spending fell 3.6% y/y, the eighth consecutive decline, the trade balance is MINUS 634 billion yen and the current account swung to MINUS 92.3 billion, so this is a hike into weakening domestic demand. Average cash earnings at 23:50Z on September 7 is the print that decides whether the yen keeps +2 into the meeting. The euro and the Aussie are unchanged and quietly the most comfortable positions on the board. The ECB moves on Thursday to a 2.50% deposit facility - fully priced on TE's calendar at 2.65% refi from 2.40% - with July accounts already on the record saying the pause was not the end of the cycle and another hike is likely unless the outlook improves significantly, and the market splitting roughly 50/50 on a further move to 2.75% in December. Area HICP is 3.3%, the highest since September 2023. Australia holds the G10-high 4.35% cash rate with September 29 around 54%, trimmed mean stuck at 3.6%, and AUD/NZD closed the week at 1.22456, up 1.03% on the week and 2.14% on the month - the single best-working idea on this board. Switzerland is untouched since Friday and holds +1, capped by the SNB's stated readiness to intervene. New Zealand stays at 0, with one honest qualification worth carrying: the RBNZ track implies a pause on October 28 and a hike to 3.00% in December, the market prices that, and a MAJORITY of MPC members - not a minority - see upside risks to inflation from persistent domestic pressure. The kiwi is still the weakest currency here, but the case against it is a shade less lopsided than it was a week ago, so keep expressing it against AUD and JPY rather than adding new legs. Finally, the war escalated again over the weekend while markets were shut, which means Monday opens with something unpriced in it: on September 5 the IRGC fired ballistic missiles toward a US aircraft carrier and a destroyer - neither hit, no casualties - and CENTCOM responded by permanently disabling two Iranian oil tankers and completely destroying a third, including the M/T Kylo in the Gulf of Oman. Vice President Vance has said there will be no talks with Iran until it stops attacking shipping. Oil should open bid.

USD.when: Sept 16, 18:00Z - back to 55-62% from the 50-55% Waller left it at, but still knife-edge and decided by CPI on Sept 11
USD.note: TE re-verified this morning: policy rate 3.75% upper bound, CPI 3.4% with MoM 0.1%, unemployment 4.1% in August, NON-FARM PAYROLLS +162,000 with the previous month revised to +21,000 from -23,000, Q2 GDP 1.5% annualised with annual growth 2.1%, average hourly earnings +0.3% m/m and 3.1% y/y, participation 61.6% from 61.4%, private payrolls +127,000, government +35,000, manufacturing payrolls +16,000, job vacancies 7,738k from 6,948k, business confidence 54.6, manufacturing PMI 53.9, non-manufacturing PMI 55.4, services PMI 56.5, consumer confidence 51.7, retail sales -0.6% m/m. USD is UPGRADED from 0 to +1 and the reason is that the premise of the dovish case was removed rather than merely offset. For a fortnight the argument for a soft dollar rested on a labour market that had printed MINUS 23,000 in July and +20,000 before that; the August report tripled a +53,000 consensus and revised the prior two months up by a combined 55,000, turning July positive. Participation rose while the unemployment rate held, which is absorption rather than deterioration. Pricing for September 16 swung back from roughly 50-55% to 55-62% across venues, the 2-year yield reached its highest since January 2025, and gold fell over 2%. The upgrade stops at +1 for one specific and important reason: Governor Waller conditioned his public case for a HOLD on inflation continuing to improve - he cited three-month annualised core PCE at 3.05% against 4.76% in February - and explicitly not on monthly payrolls, so this print does not by itself move him. Chair Warsh has separately warned that softer inflation reports have not yet shown meaningful improvement in the underlying trend. The meeting is therefore still two-sided and the resolving input is US CPI on Friday September 11 at 12:30Z, headline consensus 3.4%, preceded by PPI on September 10. A cool CPI keeps a sitting Governor arguing for a hold five days out and caps the dollar here; a hot one hands Warsh the meeting.

EUR.when: Sept 10, 12:15Z - TE carries consensus AND TE forecast at 2.65% refi from 2.40%, i.e. deposit facility 2.25% to 2.50%
EUR.note: Deposit facility re-verified on TE this morning at 2.25% (Aug 2026); the 2.40% figure is the main refi rate and 2.65% the marginal lending rate. EUR HOLDS at +2 with the forward unchanged from Friday. The July accounts, carried on TE, remain the strongest single piece of forward evidence on this board: all policymakers agreed to hold in July citing elevated uncertainty and an energy shock whose full inflationary impact had yet to emerge, but SOME would not have opposed another hike, the likelihood of further tightening becoming unnecessary remained LOW, the pause should NOT be interpreted as the end of the cycle, and another hike is likely unless the inflation outlook improves significantly - while stressing no pre-commitment to September. Thursday's 25bp move is fully priced, so the euro trades the GUIDANCE and specifically the December question: the market currently splits roughly 50/50 on a further move to 2.75% by year-end, and Eurosystem staff projections have headline inflation averaging 3.0% in 2026, 2.3% in 2027 and 2.0% in 2028. TE macro re-verified: flash HICP 3.3% from 2.9%, the highest since September 2023, MoM +0.4%; Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and 1.0% y/y from 0.5%; unemployment 6.4%; manufacturing PMI 52.7 from 51.9; services 51.6; consumer confidence -15.5 from -15.9; retail sales -0.6% m/m; trade balance +8,600mn; current account +46.9bn. The caveat that keeps this at +2 rather than +3 is unchanged: core eased to 2.4% with services at 3.0%, so the pass-through the ECB says it is watching for has not appeared. EUR/USD 1.16143, -0.10% Friday but +0.24% on the week - note that the euro HELD against a +162,000 payroll, which is the tell that its own leg is real.

GBP.when: Sept 17, 11:00Z - market-implied probability of no change is now about 90% after the DMP survey
GBP.note: Bank Rate re-verified on TE at 3.75%, held 6-3 on July 30 for a fifth consecutive meeting with Pill, Greene and Mann voting for 4.00%. GBP STAYS at 0 for a sixth session and the reason has now hardened rather than merely persisted. This file named Friday's Decision Maker Panel survey as the single specific event that would either give the three dissenters a fourth vote or take the hawkish case off the table: it printed one-year firm CPI expectations at 3.1%, DOWN from 3.4%, with three-year expectations at 2.8%. That is the dovish resolution, and market pricing for September 17 is now roughly 90% for no change. TE re-verified: business confidence at -36 from -65 - a genuine and large improvement, dated September - services PMI 52.5 from 52.1, consumer confidence -14 from -17, annual GDP growth 1.2% from 0.9%; against manufacturing PMI 51.7 from 51.9, retail sales -0.5% m/m, quarterly GDP +0.4% from +0.6%, unemployment 4.9%, CPI 2.9% with core FLAT at 2.6% for a third month, trade deficit -5,537mn. The one hawkish channel that survives is energy: UK gas is 178.81 GBp/therm and +39.65% on the MONTH into a confirmed October Ofgem cap rise, which will show up in headline CPI but has not yet moved firms expectations. Sterling therefore stays the board's cleanest funding leg against the yen, the Aussie and the euro - that is a position with a reason behind it, not a default. Cable 1.35230, -0.02% Friday and -0.09% on the week. Next UK catalyst is monthly GDP on September 11 at 06:00Z.

JPY.when: Sept 18, 03:00Z - Ueda has hinted a hike is likely and TE forecasts 1.25%; the hike is not the question, the guidance after it is
JPY.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE at 1.00%, the highest since 1995, held July 31 in an 8-1 vote with Takata dissenting for 1.25%. JPY HOLDS at +2 and remains the top of the board on the strength of the week rather than the day. USD/JPY fell 2.38% on the week to 156.254, touching roughly 155.28 intraday - a one-month high for the yen - and it was the outperformer of the G10 even into a +162,000 US payroll, which is the important tell: the yen absorbed the single most dollar-positive event of the month and still finished the week 2.4% stronger. The catalyst is intact. Ueda has hinted a hike is likely when the board convenes on September 17-18, saying he will decide with upside price risks in mind and that he hopes to discuss whether the likelihood of the BoJ scenario materialising is heightening; TE forecasts 1.25% for the meeting; Takata is pushing for consecutive moves; US Treasury Secretary Bessent met Ueda and called publicly for decisive steps on yen weakness. In the July outlook the BoJ cut FY2026 inflation to 2.5% from 2.8% but RAISED FY2027 to 2.4% from 2.3% and lifted growth for both years. The caveat is unchanged and is not diminishing: July real household spending fell 3.6% y/y against a -1.6% consensus, the EIGHTH consecutive monthly decline and the worst in more than eighteen months; the trade balance is MINUS 634bn yen and the current account swung to MINUS 92.3bn. TE macro re-verified: CPI 1.9% with MoM +0.4%, jobless rate 2.4%, retail sales +2.4% m/m, manufacturing PMI 54.9 from 54.5, services 52.5 from 51.2, consumer confidence 35.5 from 34.9, annual GDP growth 0.7%. Practical position: average cash earnings at 23:50Z on September 7, alongside final Q2 GDP and the current account, is the print that decides whether JPY carries +2 into the meeting. A miss takes it to +1 and takes JPYBASKET off.

AUD.when: Sept 29, 04:30Z - market-implied about 54%, with NAB calling September and ANZ and CBA calling November
AUD.note: Cash rate re-verified on TE at 4.35%, the G10 high, held August 11. AUD HOLDS at +2 and is the most comfortable position on this board because nothing tested it on Friday and its best expression keeps working. The package is unchanged: Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q against +0.3% expected with annual growth 2.1% against 1.8%, still above the RBA estimated 2% non-inflationary speed limit; trimmed mean stuck at 3.6% while headline eased to 3.5% from 3.8% with MoM +1.0%; the RBA saying explicitly that inflation remains too high and it could raise again if upside risks materialise. Economist positioning stays honestly split - NAB sees 25bp to 4.60% in September, ANZ and CBA see it in November, Westpac sees a hold for the rest of 2026 - and the market sits near 54%. TE re-verified: unemployment 4.5% from 4.4%, consumer confidence 88.9 from 83.9, manufacturing PMI 52.0, services 53.2 from 53.6, trade surplus 1,923mn from 2,341mn, building permits 17,687 from 18,351, current account -27,220mn, business confidence -6. RISKS, specific and unchanged: annual growth DECELERATED to 2.1% from 2.5%, employment fell 15,827 in July, and the China input is soft with copper -1.58% on the month. AUD/USD 0.72040, +0.05% Friday, +0.54% on the week and +2.06% on the month - still the best major of the month, and it held that against a payroll beat. AUD/NZD closed 1.22456, +1.03% on the week and +2.14% on the month, and remains the single best-working idea here.

NZD.when: Oct 28, 01:00Z is a pause; the published track and market pricing both point to the next 25bp on Dec 9 to 3.00%
NZD.note: OCR re-verified on TE at 2.75% after the September 2 hike, the second consecutive move, delivered unanimously. NZD STAYS at 0 and remains the weakest currency on the board, but this note carries one honest upgrade to the reasoning rather than to the score. The published track reaching 2.81% for Q4 2026 is exactly consistent with an unchanged October 28 and a 25bp hike to 3.00% on December 9, and the market now prices that move - so the kiwi is not being ignored by its own central bank, it is being scheduled. Further, the September Monetary Policy Statement records that a MAJORITY of MPC members see upside risks to inflation from persistent domestic pressure, and the Bank revised UP its inflation forecasts for next year; BNZ has the OCR eventually reaching 4% by May 2027 and some banks look for hikes in September, October and December to 3.25%. That is a less lopsided case than the four-of-seven framing carried earlier in the week and it is the reason not to add new short-kiwi legs here. What has NOT changed is the relative position: New Zealand has the board HIGHEST headline inflation at 4.1% and its weakest currency, because the RBNZ hiked and then said further increases are possible but not locked in, attributing the inflation rate largely to Middle East fuel prices while judging core, wages and expectations consistent with a return to the 1-3% band by mid-2027. TE re-verified: unemployment 5.6% from 5.4% and the highest since Q3 2015, manufacturing PMI 54.3 from 60.1, consumer confidence 80.4 from 94.7, business confidence 53.7 from 56.1, retail sales -0.5% m/m, trade balance MINUS 1,949mn from -237mn, GDP +0.8% q/q with annual growth 1.5%. CAD.when: Oct 28 with the MPR - DOWNGRADED from hike to hold after August employment fell 41,700 and wage growth decelerated
CAD.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE at 2.25%, held September 2 for a seventh straight meeting, unanimous across all 35 economists polled. CAD is DOWNGRADED from +2 to +1 and the leg that broke should be named precisely: it is the CENTRAL-BANK leg, not the commodity leg. August employment fell 41,700 against a +15,000 consensus after +75,100 in July, with full-time down 35,900 and part-time down 5,800; losses ran through business, building and other support services -2.8%, utilities -3.5%, natural resources -2.3% and public administration -0.7%, with only manufacturing adding at +1.2%. Wage growth decelerated. Macklem said on September 2 that the Bank is prepared to raise and that if it takes more than one increase it is prepared to do that - but he also said the uncertain outlook prevents clear signals on policy this year, and a 41,700 job loss with cooling wages is exactly the kind of slack evidence that makes a near-term hike unlikely. The mitigation, and it is real: the unemployment rate HELD at 6.4%, its lowest since 2024, participation slipped to 65.0%, and the Q2 growth number is untouched at +3.3% ANNUALISED with quarterly growth 0.8% and annual 1.1% - still the best in the G10. TE macro re-verified: CPI 3.0% with MoM +0.5%, current account +8,800mn, business confidence 64.3 UP sharply from 55.1, manufacturing PMI 53.0 from 53.5, consumer confidence 48.2 from 49.4, retail sales -0.8% m/m, trade surplus 770mn from 4,200mn. The COMMODITY leg is stronger than at any point this cycle: WTI settled 91.48 for a weekly gain near 9.7%, its best week since mid-July, Brent 96.28 and +21.18% on the month, and the war escalated again on September 5. That is why CAD lands at +1 rather than 0. Practical consequence: USD/CAD goes from HIGH-conviction SHORT to RANGE, GBP/CAD and NZD/CAD drop to LOW-MED, and C$27.6bn of counter-tariffs across roughly 700 US product lines take effect on September 8.

CHF.when: Sept 24, 07:30Z - TE carries a 0% consensus and nothing since Friday changes the base case
CHF.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE at 0.00%, held March 19 and June 18. CHF HOLDS at +1, unchanged, with no new Swiss data since Friday. The two upside surprises from last week both stand: August CPI at 0.8% y/y against a 0.5% consensus and TE own 0.6% forecast, up from 0.4% in July and the fastest since August 2024, with core rising to 0.4% from 0.3% - its first increase of the year - and the monthly rate at +0.4% after -0.1%; and the final Q2 GDP revision at +1.5% q/q with ANNUAL growth revised up to 2.3% from 0.4%, the strongest quarterly growth since Q3 2021, led by chemicals and pharmaceuticals with value added rising across a wide range of sectors. Two beats in three days is a real change of state. What keeps it at +1 rather than +2 is unchanged and structural: the SNB June guidance forecasts annual average inflation of just 0.6% for 2026 AND 2027 and 0.7% for 2028 with growth around 1% for 2026, the Bank said medium-term inflation pressures remain largely unchanged despite energy-driven price increases, TE carries a 0% consensus for September 24 with no forecast for a move, and critically the SNB signalled GREATER READINESS TO INTERVENE in FX markets while explicitly naming Middle East tensions as something that could strengthen the franc. That is a stated policy ceiling, and this weekend escalation makes it more relevant rather than less. TE macro re-verified: unemployment 3.0% from 2.9%, manufacturing PMI 57.1 from 53.2, business confidence 107 from 104, trade surplus 8,141mn from 3,834mn, retail sales +0.1% m/m, consumer confidence -35 from -36, current account 15,544mn. USD/CHF 0.80979, +0.28% Friday and +0.24% on the week - the franc gave ground to the dollar on payrolls, as it should with the Fed axis turning. Keep CHF pairs at MEDIUM or below and do not buy a hawkish SNB.

catalysts.event: Japan average cash earnings + final Q2 GDP + current account
catalysts.note: The single most important print before the BoJ. With household spending down 3.6% y/y for an eighth straight month, cash earnings now carries the entire wage-price case behind the September 18 hike on its own. A miss is the specific event that takes JPY from +2 to +1 and takes JPYBASKET off - and it would do it before the meeting rather than after.

catalysts.note: Bessent met Ueda and called publicly for decisive monetary steps on yen weakness. With USD/JPY having touched about 155.28 and the BoJ expected to hike, the intervention risk is now asymmetric - a hawkish surprise needs no help, a dovish one invites it.

The SNB signalled in June a greater readiness to intervene in FX markets, naming Middle East tensions as something that could strengthen the franc. That is the stated ceiling keeping CHF at +1 despite two upside data surprises, and the weekend escalation is exactly the scenario the Bank described.

geopolitics: The war escalated materially over the weekend and markets have not traded it yet, which is the single most important thing about Monday open. On September 5 Iran Revolutionary Guard Corps navy launched ballistic missiles toward a US aircraft carrier and a destroyer; neither ship was hit and no servicemembers were injured. CENTCOM responded by permanently disabling two Iranian oil tankers and completely destroying a third, including the M/T Kylo in the Gulf of Oman, under the tanker-for-tanker policy President Trump approved earlier this month. The IRGC says it targeted three tankers sailing an unauthorised route through the Strait of Hormuz plus three US-affiliated vessels elsewhere. That follows the September 2 strikes on roughly 60 targets, the first US strikes on Iranian TANKERS of the war, in which two Filipino sailors were killed aboard Bahri SIDR. Vice President Vance has stated there will be no peace talks with Iran until it stops attacking ships in Hormuz, which removes the negotiation path traders were pricing a fortnight ago. The price context going in was already strong: WTI settled 91.48 on Friday for a weekly gain near 9.7%, its best week since mid-July, with Brent 96.28; on the month WTI is +21.62% and Brent +21.18%. The drivers named by the market were renewed US-Iran exchanges, continued Hormuz restrictions, falling US crude inventories and an exceptionally tight diesel market, with Israel defence minister separately threatening crippling attacks on Iranian energy infrastructure. The offsetting force remains demand rather than supply: OPEC has cut its 2026 global oil demand growth estimate to 580,000 barrels per day from 780,000, and throughput recovery is the specific thing that would drain the premium. Four FX consequences follow. First, and this is the change from last week, the oil leg NO LONGER carries the Canadian dollar on its own: with employment down 41,700 and wage growth cooling, the BoC leg has failed, so crude strength keeps CAD at +1 rather than restoring it to +2 - USD/CAD becomes a range rather than a short, and the honest read is that a Canada trade now needs the oil argument to do all the work. Second, the tightening board foundation is intact and getting reinforcement: the ECB July accounts explicitly cite Middle East upside inflation risk, the BoC statement cites the continuation of the war, and the SNB named Middle East tensions as a franc-strengthening risk in June, so these reaction functions keep working. Third, the franc ceiling becomes more relevant rather than less - a haven bid into a Hormuz escalation is precisely the scenario the SNB described when it signalled greater readiness to intervene, which is why CHF stays capped at +1 and why the CHF crosses stay at MEDIUM or below despite good Swiss data. Fourth, the yen terms-of-trade problem keeps deteriorating: Japan imports essentially all its oil, the trade balance is MINUS 634 billion yen, the current account swung to MINUS 92.3 billion, and July household spending fell 3.6% year-on-year with energy and food costs named as the cause. The BoJ is therefore hiking into a shock that strengthens its inflation argument and weakens its demand base at the same time - which is exactly why average cash earnings on Monday night matters more than any other print this week.
